| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |

raw_comment: This graph is supposed to convey the effects of social distancing. Coronavirus infects the world like a chain. If a single link is intact, the virus continues to spread and the chain will carry on. Yet, if a link is broken, the chain stops. By staying at home and keeping to yourself, you can break the chain. As much as I would like to think that after a few months of social distancing this will all go away, I know it is not a reality. The big question throughout this pandemic still remains; if and when will things be normal again?

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment: I noticed how this graph has two parts. In the first graph, we can see how the virus is spreading quickly and to more people. It started with one person that had the virus and goes in contact with two others that also get the virus. These two people also get in contact with two other people each, and those with two more. This cycle keeps happening until the virus is spread or until we take precautions. However, in the second graph, we see how thanks to social distancing, the first person only infects one person instead of two. That is also saving a lot of people from getting the virus. So this graph is saying that if we keep distance between people we can save hundreds of others. I still wonder how this graph works in reality and how we can figure out. Also, I am wondering how could we spread this message to make everyone realize that we need to take precautions until the virus stops spreading.

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

You only saw two people it should be fine, but what goes unaccounted for at the moment is the people who then see those newly infected people. it becomes a chain reaction. 

I wonder if people take into account the fact that the people they are in context with are also in contact with other people. of course, this results in the virus spreading but are people aware they are in contact with the more people then they know(the other people that the person they saw was in contact with)?

how social distance can slow the spread of the virus

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |

raw_comment:
After reading the reveal, the animation in particular stood out to me. All of the mundane tasks that people were staying out of in the animation really showed how much social distancing actually matters. 

It made me think back to last day that nonessential businesses were still open in New Hampshire. I had to get parts for a project I was working on so I took that day to go around and stock up. Everywhere I went, I social distanced as best as possible. One situation in particular stood out to me, though. When I was at Home Depot, a guy was walking towards me down the aisle. Upon seeing each other, we changed which side of the aisle that we were walking on. We were both left, then both right, then both left again, etc. At the time, it was super awkward, but we both laughed it off, knowing what each other was doing.

The reveal makes me think about how, no matter how awkward that situation was, it's entirely possible (if not realistic) that if either of us were carrying the virus we help lessen the load on nearly a hundred people.

raw_comment:
I enjoyed reading the reveal. It opened my eyes to how people from all around the globe can come together to form and share like ideas. These ideas can be co impactful and represent the future minds of our planet. The revealed painted an image of how math can be tied into a pandemic and really pushed for the idea of social distancing. The reveal was very meaningful because it's a way of using evidence to show a message, social distancing will drastically slow the spread of coronavirus.
         Furthermore, I liked reading other students' and scholars' titles for the graphs. I loved the creativity! Also, the exponential growth model was a great way to express in a clear way the harm of not following social distancing. I think that it is important to address how it can be difficult to make an accurate model when there are still so many unknowns that exist regarding the virus. However, this reveal provides great evidence to back up why social distancing is critical.

raw_comment:
The reveal accentuates the importance of social distancing to suppress the spread of the virus.  Last week's reveal regarded the importance of "flattening the curve" to prevent overwhelming our nation's healthcare system.  The coronavirus chain of transmission in this week's reveal explains the need to social distance, prevent the transmission of coronavirus, and as a result protect our healthcare system from becoming overwhelmed.
I really enjoyed watching the attached animation that explicitly demonstrates the importance of staying home.  Because of the exponential growth in the animation, the impact constantly increases as people fail to social distance.  The animation also shows the essential actions that need to be taken as soon as the virus enters an area.  The sooner the first patient is identified, the spread of the virus will be significantly reduced.

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment:
My favorite part of this reveal was the animation that went along with it. Before the reveal, the graph showed how important is was to keep your social distance because of how easily it spreads. This graph was one that grew exponentially. The animation in the reveal showed the same graph, but also showed what would happen if some people kept their distance from others. It displayed a drastic change in the number of people who would be infected. It's one thing to hear why it is important to stay at home and keep our distance from others, but its importance is inflated through this visual. 
The reveal also brought up that it is extremely difficult to create a good model of COVID-19. This makes sense to me because there is an abundance of both known and unknown confounding factors that get in the way of trying to find the true data.

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

This article shows over and over again the importance of staying home and social distancing. It shows graphs of different scenerios that could happen. If not everyone participates in social distancing, than the virus will continue to spread.

|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |

raw_comment: According to my observations from this graph, one person can infect two people and each of them can expose two more people. It's like an ongoing cycle. This disclosure further supports the idea of social distancing. However it makes me wonder that if people are aware of the consequences due to interactions, why  then won't they separate themselves from others? ## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |
raw_comment:
When I analyzed the animation, I noticed that when one person stayed home or distanced themselves a whole section of the chain of people being infected after the first person was eliminated off of the chain. When just one person decides to take action and take the precautions that society has been told to follow they have now prevented many others from infection.
When creating the proposed tree graphs for each scenario I noticed that when each person was around three people at stage three there were twenty seven people infected by the end of stage three. When further analyzing the tree graphs I noticed an exponential equation occurring. The equation works by taking the number of people each person is around and raising it to the power of x, the stage that you are solving for, this would give you the number of people infected at the stage plugged in. For example, when each person was around one person you could raise one to the fourth power to find that that at that stage one more person was infected. Another is when each person was around three people you could find three to the power of three would give you twenty seven which is the number of people in stage three that were infected on the tree graph providing evidence for the equation that was built.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment:
The Reveal explained the truth behind the graph- how by reducing our social contacts, we can reduce the spread and severity of the virus. The story that the animation tells us highlights what experts are telling us nationwide: if you stay home, and choose to remove yourself from the social contact of others, you will exponentially stop the spread of the virus. When we come in contact with one person, we run the risk of infecting many more people than just the two we may see. I appreciate that the Reveal highlights how difficult it is to accurately model how people’s interaction cause a spread in the virus. This is because people’s contact patterns differ so greatly and we don’t always know what people would be infected. 
	The tree diagram was a very useful model for this data because without doing many calculations, the viewer can draw conclusions that the scientists want you to see. Exponential growth is quite easy to recognize as each branch doubles so that the entire tree is multiplying in size. This diagram also makes the reader think about their personal choices - if you choose to see just one fewer person, you may reduce the number of infections by 64 people. This adds a realistic sense of why we have so much personal responsibility in slowing the pandemic.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |
raw_comment:
I notice that even the interaction between you and just two of your friends can cause a large butterfly effect in which many people get infected, which seems very concerning due to the fact that most of us are around a lot of people everyday. So in the end, this proves how social isolation can be very beneficial, and can reduce spread. I mean, imagine this graph with 4 other human interactions, imagine how many people could get infected then.

I wonder why this graph is only limited to two physical social interactions, instead of more, as you we as humans normally interact with many many more people per day. So that brings up another question, is this during the quarantine, or afterwards, because if this was during quarantine this would make a lot of sense, but if it was before, would this graph just be trying to show us how easily this virus can spread through just two interactions with other people.

I guess a catchy headline could be, "The butterfly effect of Coronavirus" (sorry if this is bad, I'm not that great with making titles such as this one)

raw_comment:
My headline- Just staying home could save many lives, including your own. 
I truly wonder why people aren't staying home. In the last few weeks, many different people, from the president to doctors to teachers to governors, are trying so hard just to get people to stay home. As backed up by this graph, if people would stay home unless they need food or an emergency, than the spread of the coronavirus will diminish by great numbers. I think that many people's mindset is that "I don't have the disease, so if I go out and do what I want then it's fine". Part of staying at home is protecting yourself, as well. However, this graph blew my mind as to how much just 1 person can change the spread.

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

This makes me think that social distancing is the best way to stop the virus because it will not be spreading as fast.

raw_comment:
I noticed that as the virus spreads from person to person, its growth increases exponentially. The graph shows the spread and rate of affliction of the coronavirus. As seen in the graph, the first person spreads it to two people, and then those two people spread it to two other people, and so on. This makes it extremely hard to stop the virus in its tracks because of how contagious it is and how difficult it is to stop the spread. If the virus is not stopped early, then more people will unfortunately be afflicted with the illness. This graph makes me wonder how to stop the spread of the virus. In the second visual, it shows how if Patient Zero was to not make contact with one of the potential carriers, then the number of people afflicted with the virus would be cut in half. Because of this information, I wonder how people can stop the spread of the virus, and it leads me to think that the best way to defeat it is through social distancing and not making any sort of contact with people. raw_comment: To me this graph depicts how social distancing can prohibit COVID-19 from affecting other people. One graph shows how fast COVID-19 spreads from person to person. The other graph shows how little harm COVID-19 can do if society distances itself. The graph is a great visual representation of how people going out and touching things can be deadly. It also shows how the people who don’t know they have the virus or even people who tested positive can negatively affect the community. I wonder what the graph would look like if people distanced themselves? I also wonder how COVID-19 can be slowed down or even stopped? What does humanity have to do to eliminate this virus? What has to happen for people to realize that social distancing helps and that gathering doesn’t?

raw_comment:
I notice that there are white circles that get increasingly darker as it goes down, and that there are two colors of lines; red and grey. I believe that the circles each represent an individual human as there are silhouettes of people above the first three circles, and the red lines represent infection while grey represents uninfected individuals. It says "infection avoided" in the second picture, which is why I believe this.

I wonder if more people saw this graph then would that affect their choices in life? I think this visual representation is brilliant and really shows the gravity of each individual choice you make, and so if this was shown to one hundred people how many of them would then decide to practice more social distancing? I am curious what the actual rate of infection is however, as this implies that every single person an infected individual comes in contact with is also then infected, which I do not believe is true (although it depends).

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |
raw_comment:
What this graph shows to me is what social distancing does and how effective it is. If there is social distancing then infections will be avoided. On the graph, it shows that when an infection is bypassed a whole branch of people will be safe from the virus. But, when the virus is spread to another, they will have the same problem as the starting person, there are two people that can be infected and the outcome depends on social distancing The graph is as large as our population, meaning that in the beginning, if someone is not avoided then a whole bunch of people will be infected, kind of like a chain reaction. This graph is exponential because every person who gets infected can infect two more people, and then they can infect two more, etc. 

This shows how social distancing helps to contain the spread of Corona and other viruses. 

A good title would be: "To isolate or not not to isolate: what is the difference?"

In this graph, I noticed three main people, one person in red that started the domino effect and two other people who got the virus from the first person. I also noticed that the red lines connecting each person represent the virus spreading to the people. I wonder how much different it would be if social distancing will actually result in what the second graph shows on the right hand side. 

I would call this article: The Red Effect.right-hand

raw_comment: This graphic provides a clear visual of the role each individual plays in the spread of COVID-19. For every person with whom the infected individual avoids contact, an entire branch of exponential growth is eliminated, greatly reducing the number of people who contract the virus. In the real world, the individual depicted actually wields much more power. This is because the majority of humans have a vast network of people with whom they would typically come in close contact. In the graphic, the removal of one interaction prevents 63 total cases. If we imagine the average person would interact with 10 different people rather than 2, this number jumps to an astounding 111,111. This means that one person limiting their physical contact could prevent a fifth of the population of Wyoming from contracting a life-threatening disease, likely saving over 700 lives. It is important to take into account that these are only potential infections, as not everybody who comes in contact with the disease will be infected. I am curious how long this pattern and rate of spread can continue within a certain region or area, as the entire world population would theoretically be infected by 2^33 (the spread slows eventually). I would like to point out that the WHO recommends the term "physical distancing" over "social distancing", as it's more accurate and doesn't carry the same negative implications of isolation. I would title this graph "The Power of Physical Distancing: How You Can Save Lives".

raw_comment:
I noticed that the spread of the Coronavirus is exponential, with a growth factor of 2. The number of infected people doubles at a single contact, which is why the 'curve' of the illness rises so rapidly. The diagram also exhibits the effectiveness of social distancing, since when one of the two original people avoid infection, the entire infected population at the end is reduced by 50%. 
I am curious about how the diagram would change if there were a way to incorporate a recovery rate. How would social distancing affect recoveries? What if you could get it twice?

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

I wonder how the graph would look if every time you can in contact with someone, you didn't necessarily get infected.

raw_comment: I noticed the impact of social distancing. Since the transmission of this virus is exponential, by the sixth stage, 64 new people have it, adding on to the 62 people from the last 5 stages. If this goes on, hundreds of thousands of people can get it, as we can have seen in our daily lives. Even reducing contact with one person can save many from getting infected, cutting the infection rate in half. However, this model is not a totally accurate representation of the scenario. It shows that one person will infect two more people. However, one person can transfer to three people, or four, as many as they meet. All it takes is the transfer of droplets through personal contact or sneezing. I wonder how this model would be changed if the number of people the virus was transmitted to was randomized. Definitely, more people would be infected, and impact of social distancing would be different. I would name this article "Social Distancing: Why You Shouldn't Go to the Beach"

raw_comment:
The first thing I notice is the huge difference there is between the end number of people infected between the two graphs. By just eliminating one person in the chain, you can save many from potentially being infected. Each person goes out and infects two more people, causing this disease to spread exponentially rather than linearly. I wonder how accurate that number is, and if cutting out one social interaction really makes as much difference as shown in the graph. 

Social distancing is very important to fighting this disease, and we need to take it seriously. The number of infected people will eventually slow down, but we can make sure that we have the ability to treat all the sick people in the meantime with these preventative measures. If everyone took these lockdowns seriously and only had contact with their immediate family, the effects could be greatly reduced. 

I’ve heard people say that it doesn’t matter if they are just going to hang out with one person. But just like in the graph, that one person could’ve gotten infected from one other person they were previously with. You can’t control the interactions of the people around you, so you just have to control yours and make sure you aren’t unnecessarily putting yourself and others at risk.

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment:
We have been moderating for 5 hours and there have been 559 responses with over 100 great headlines.  Thanks to all students who responded.  And, just as importantly, to the students who replied to other students.  You made this a community in these times of school closings and social isolation.  Here are a small group of catchy headlines that capture the main idea of this graph:  "One Person Makes a Difference" by Gabrielle and "Small Actions Prevent Large Numbers" by Ethan, both from Akron, Ohio, “Coronavirus Cases Could Be Cut in Half If You Do This One Easy Thing!” by Gabriel of Polaris Expeditionary Learning School in Fort Collins, Colorado, and “Coronavirus Chain Explained!” by Jada of the Big Island, Hawai’i, "How one person can end a pandemic"  by Madison, FL and "Social Distancing: Double or Nothing" by Deven,  Portsmouth NH.
You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, April 2 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a few Stat Nuggets.

Check out a cool giphy I found on this.https://giphy.com/gifs/LM97YWpnbTp85Du7aA

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:

  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |

raw_comment: I notice that every graph shows the effects that the spread of COVID-19 have with and without social distancing. The first graph shows that a single person is likely to give it to 2 other people. This branches into many others contracting it because  of how quickly and easily it can be caught. The second graph shows the effects social distancing has on the spread of the virus. The person at the start of the graph only gave it to one other person, saving a whole branch full of people from contracting the virus. Coronavirus is exponentially increasing and social distancing/quarantining ourselves is truly helping. I wonder how many people will catch the virus even if they took all the necessary precautions. I wonder hoe many carriers there are who do not have any visible symptoms. I wonder how long the limits on social contact will be in place.

- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment:
I notice that a lot fewer people are infected when a person decides to self-isolate. This can be seen by the graph as if both people infected by the red person decide not to self isolate then the potential number of people to be infected (as seen on the graph) is sixty-four. But if one of the two infected people decides to self isolate then the number goes down to thirty-two. If both people decide to self-isolate then the number goes down to two, as in the two self-isolating people. If the original person decides to self-isolate then, the number decreases to one, that person. By each person who decides to self-isolate the number of possible infected people goes down by half.
I wonder if there is any way to avoid the first person getting infected at all? I also wonder if we had handled the initial start of the disease, by immediately starting to self-isolate internationally, how would the numbers have changed? 
A total for this graph could be "How self-isolating decreases the amount of cases."

A cool headline could be "The Viral Virus".

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

dependency_graph.reasoning: Step 4a: 'Should' directly recommends action.

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

## 1) Chart type

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment: I notice that this display predicts that every person will spread the virus to two other people. Assuming each dot represents one case of the virus, there happen to be 127 cases in the top half of the display. Each of those cases branched off from one person, which shows that a little leads to a lot in terms of this virus. So what would happen if each person instead spread the virus to three other people? If this were true and the virus multiplied six times like it did in this display, there would be a whopping 1093 total cases of the virus (that's 1+3+3^2+3^3+3^4+3^5+3^6) instead of 127. If everyone spread it to FOUR other people, this number would be 5461. This scares me because it might be possible that many people would spread the virus to three or four other people, since it seems like many people are not staying distant from their friends during these times. This provides strong evidence that staying socially distant from others is very important in times like these, and that all people should be taking social distancing practices seriously, because if both of the first two infections were avoided, this virus chain would have ended at the first person. I wonder if it is really true that each person spreads the virus to only two other people, because it seems like lots of essential workers that cannot work from home would come into contact with many more than two other people over the course of even a day. A catchy headline could be "Social Distancing: Double or Nothing"

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

I noticed that when one person chooses to self isolate, they can save over 10 times as many people from getting the virus. When one person chooses to go out, they don't just put themselves at risk, but everyone they pass by, talk to, and their family, then those people do the same and the cycle continues. If we all self isolated, the virus would pass much quicker, and affect fewer number of people.

    A catchy headline that shows the graph's main idea could be, "How one person can end a pandemic"

I promised many of my students I would share their thoughts.

Here's another:

"I think it talks about how avoiding contact with people helps reduce the number of people getting infected with the virus. I believe this because I notice at the bottom it states infection avoided and the lines are all connected just like all the people that have the coronavirus have a link. I wonder if the infection is avoided, does it reduce the number of cases by half? A headline for the graph would be Coronavirus Links."

Another:

"I notice that the graph shows a chain on how the Coronavirus can spread fast and easily, and how it can stop spreading that fast. The part of the graph that makes me think that, is that on the graph there is one where one person spreads the virus to another, and it goes on. The other part of the graph shows how half the people could not get the virus, because the person decided to isolate themselves. I wonder how long will it take to know that that many people have gotten the virus? I also wonder if isolation is the best way to not spread the virus? A catchy phrase could be, "Isolate and you won't spread or get"."

raw_comment: I find these two graphs very fascinating. With the data, I can come to the conclusion that social distancing from one another can reduce about 50% of the coronavirus infections that usually happen when you are around others in public places. In the second graph, the person on the far right avoids the infected person by social distancing or staying at home, so that they do not contact others, and the people surrounding the infected people. When one person avoids contacting an infected person, they reduce the chance of passing it down to a whole other group of people, that keep chaining to affect everyone one by one. People who do hang out with this infected person, may not know that the person they are with is infected. Right now, if everyone started to distance themselves with others, there could be a major change, which can decrease the virus spreading significantly.

raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the impact of limiting social contacts, as mentioned in the title.The red person demonstrates one infected with the corona virus, and the gray people represent people that the person in red could interact with. Each of the people that could be infected interact with a chain of others that interact with a large chain of others that can also be infected. I notice that the more interaction occurs, the more the chance for infection increases, as the gray circles increase in number towards the bottom of the chain. I also notice that when someone infected does not physically interact with a non infected person, the chain of people that can later be infected is cut off. I wonder what makes the COVID-19 disease so contagious? Possible Title: "Separate, Stop the Spread, Stay Safe"

sentence_classifications.image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |

raw_comment:
In this graph, I notice that each graph shows the effects of the spread of the virus with and without social distancing. The first graph shows that a person infected is likely to give it to 2 people. This stems into thousands because of how quickly and easy you can contract the virus. The second graph shows the effects of social distancing on the virus. The initial person who had the virus only gave it to one person instead of 2. This cut half the people in half who will contract the virus, showing that social distancing does truly help. I wonder how many people contract the virus even taking the precautions advised. In addition, I wonder how many people are carriers without showing any symptoms vs. the people who have it and show symptoms.

Welcome to our moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  Last week, we had a graph that showed how “flattening the curve” could reduce the number of infected people at any one time in our healthcare system.  This week, we have two graphs that show the effect of protective measures on reducing the number of infected people.  

This graph is a tree diagram.  It is a model and is not based on data.  It shows how many people could be infected given some assumptions.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph. 

We encourage students to respond to other students.  We expect teachers to respond to their students as well other students from around the world.

Before Friday, we will reveal the article that included this graph and much more.

I notice the graph is displaying how social distancing can flatten the curve of the coronavirus. There are two graphs shown. The first graph shows what occurs when social distancing takes place. When that third person is infected, it is not only them. That person then infects many other people. However, in the second graph, it shows how many people would not be infected if the third person properly socially distanced themselves. Since the coronavirus spreads through direct touch and does not spread through the air, social distancing is so highly recommended. If you are not staying quarantined for yourself, then you must think about the other people or the elders that you could infect and potentially kill.

I wonder how long the quarantine would last if people stopped leaving their houses, or if they actually practiced a safe 6 feet distance from people?

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:

  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

Title: "(F.R.I.E.N.D.S) I won't be there for you" 

The graph displays the difference one person makes on spreading the coronavirus. In the first graph, just three people interacting exponentially spreads the virus, but in the second graph, because the third person "stayed home" or did not meet up with the other two, half of the people from the first graph that contracted it did not. raw_comment: I notice that what people need in times like these isn't a suggestion, it isn't telling someone to stop going out because it dangerous, its a stern and impactful warning, along with repercussions on breaking said warning consecutively. I'm not implying every country to enact a law where if you go out without a mask you should be persecuted.  As much as that would reduce the number of any more potential infected. People fail to acknowledge that its not only their lives in danger, its the lives of their loved ones, their friends, their families that are in danger as well. I turned 20 recently, and I know that cases of death in my age range are almost abysmal really because of our immune systems better fare than others, so even if I do catch it, its almost going to be like a bad cold. However, that doesn't mean my parents and my little brother who's immune system is weaker than mine will be experiencing the same thing. I notice in that graph, those who walk around infecting more and even more people, are none other than those who think they're safe and they are, but... not really. I wonder, to those individuals in the graphs that spread the virus. What they are thinking, and I want to tell to them, "You realize that because you weren't aware enough of the situation, people who died because they were weaker and unable fight back the virus, that their blood is on your hands?". In that graph I see "Carelessness, Ignorance, and Self-Consciousness".

| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment:
I noticed that by limiting social contact, transmission will also be limited. The graph shows one red/infected person on the peek, then connects two adjoining red lines to two other people. These two people are colored gray suggesting that they are not infected but exposed. This means that they are definitely carrying the virus with them but are asymptomatic. These two people then individually spread it to two different people; who each also spread it to two more people; and so on. This means that even if the person is not symptomatic they may still be a carrier of the virus. If social contact decreases, then the likelihood of spreading the disease decreases. 

I wonder here in South Korea how many people would have actually been infected had they not limited social contact. As of April 1, the majority of new cases are from travelers coming from abroad. 

How Broad Will the Coronavirus Chain of Transmission Umbrella Become?

- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

There are many ways that even if just one of these grey dots decided to stay home. ## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |
