image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

|---|---|---|

| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:

  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |
raw_comment: I notice that, even though the first person is only coming into contact with two people, they are unknowingly affecting many more than two people. I also noticed that, compared to the second graph where the person is limiting the interactions they have with other people by seeing one less person, they actually significantly decrease the number of people they are infecting in the end. I feel as though this number would probably be higher given that most people are staying inside with their families of more than 2 people, meaning they would likely infect them as well if they were going out and not social distancing. A catchy headline could be "Not social distancing: who are you infecting?"

In the graphs posted, I noticed that, when using social distancing or self-quarantining, you can cut about 50% of infections that typically occur in daily contact with others around you. You can see this by when the person on the far right avoids the infected person, distancing themselves or quarantining themselves, they don't come in contact with the other person as well as the other people  surrounding them. When this one person avoids contact with the infected person they don't pass it down the chain of people. The people who are going around this person may not know that the person infected is in fact, infected.
I wonder what would happen to the current societal situation if everyone started to distance themselves and not come in contact with other people as much. Instead of going to the grocery store, maybe order what you need online and have it delivered right to your door step preventing in-store workers from infection and limiting the number of people out and about. These delivery workers are already going to be out and walking around so others staying inside or away would also decrease their chance of getting the virus like the graph shows. All of those people after that one person won't get infected if just one person stays back!
Catchy Headline: One Person Makes a Big Difference

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment:
I notice how by keeping ones distance from another person the infection is avoided and therefore leading to a plethora of other cases being prevented. The first chart shows the person infecting two people and each time that person interacted, two more people became infected. The chain continues to expand and at the bottom of the first chart there are 64 cases just because one person did not follow the protective measures. When the person only interacted with one person the number of cases were cut in half. 
I wonder why so many people still refuse to obey the social distancing guidelines. I understand it is difficult to be apart from loved ones and friends, but the whole world is feeling the exact same way. It is extremely apparent especially after observing these graphs that social distancing is vital. I wonder why people continue to disregard important information like this. Social distancing will save lives and although it's challenging to be apart from those you care about, it is necessary. 
Catchy Headline: Distance Makes All the Difference

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:

  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.

- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts

- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

raw_comment: One noticing that I had when looking at this diagram was the dramatic decrease of people infected from the first graph to the second. In the first graph/diagram, I believe it's demonstrating society and the number of people infected without social distancing, and in the second graph I believe it is demonstrating how even one person stepping out of the chain of contamination causes dramatic effects and keeps people healthier, while slowing the spread of viruses. one thing I am wondering about is precisely how much the spread will slow, and if taking measures like this will eventually stop the spread of viruses, or just slow them to a point to were they could be contained. I am also curious as to when in history measures like this have been applied, and how effective they have proven to be. All in all I think this is a really neat explanation of social distancing, and why it is effective. I hope to better understand how effective these precautions are, and what we have learned from them in the past.

When social distancing is neglected, the virus quickly spreads from person to person, and no mercy is shown by the coronavirus.

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |
raw_comment: I notice that both scenarios in this graph start with merely one person. And after only 6 stages of transmission, 126 individuals are infected with a disease that has a mortality rate double than that of the flu. In other words, it only takes one person to set off an onslaught of disease, destruction, and death. On the other hand, social distancing measures can cut the rate of infection by a whopping half. In the second diagram, where the initial carrier of covid-19 only transmitted the virus to one person instead of two, 63 new individuals are infected, as opposed to 126 from the first diagram. This highlights the dire importance of social distancing in a disease outbreak, such as the one we are currently facing. Every transmission can lead to tens, hundreds and even thousands more. I wonder if this graph represents the person-to-person spread of the virus (through coughing and droplets in the air) only, as opposed to the transmission that can occur when the virus resides on surfaces that people touch. If so, how much worse does it get when the latter type of transmission is factored in? The headline I would choose for this graph is “The Power of One.”

raw_comment: I notice that this graph shows only if an infected person were to come into contact with only two other people. This graph would be more extreme, and maybe more realistic in some ways (at least for when the virus first began and when people were still going out to big gatherings), if it showed what would happen if a person went to a big gathering and came into contact with 50 people. I also notice that this graph grows exponentially. This graph demonstrates the importance of social distancing and the bad effects it can have not just on the people you see directly and come into contact with, but the people they come into contact with, and so on. I wonder if/when there will be a point where the corona virus does not spread exponentially anymore, or at least at a slower rate. I wonder how far in the future this will be. This all depends on if people will take social distancing seriously, if proper equipment such as masks and tests are given out to the hospitals that need it, and if people stay as healthy as they possibly can. The catchy title that comes to mind when I think of this graph is "Why It's So Important To Keep Your Social Distance"

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

## 1) Chart type
- **Node-link tree / branching transmission diagram** comparing two transmission scenarios.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.
- Not a standard axis-based chart; **no faceting grid**, but effectively a **two-panel comparative layout**.
- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |
| Interrupted/avoided infection | Categorical/nominal | Black “X” mark and red label “Infection avoided”; faded nodes/links to the right |

- **Two vertically stacked panels** (top and bottom) showing a comparison:
  - **Top:** transmission without limiting social contacts
  - **Bottom:** transmission with limiting social contacts
- Uses a **hierarchical tree layout** with branching links.

- Uses **fading/de-emphasis** and an **“X” annotation** in the lower panel to indicate interrupted transmission.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Transmission scenario (without vs. with limiting social contacts) | Categorical/nominal | Vertical panel position (top vs. bottom), subtitle/context |
| Individual/person (node in chain) | Categorical/nominal | Circle marks and person icons |
| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |

|---|---|---|

| Transmission link / infection path | Categorical/nominal | Connecting line segments between nodes |
| Generation / step in transmission chain | Ordinal | Hierarchical position in the tree (top-to-bottom levels) |
| Branching extent / number of downstream infections | Quantitative | Number of child nodes and overall spread/width of the tree |

I am a teacher at The Storm King School. I have students from Russia and China. *These are my students' opinions only I understand that there is a mask shortage, and that we should make sure that all hospitals have enough masks before they are available to the general public. Here is their advice or cautionary tales about the virus: 

Alex from Moscow, Russia says: In Russia are only getting worse right now. Quarantine in Moscow starts on Monday the 30th. Right now though, you can see a lot of people without masks and not washing hands. We could prevent the virus by doing simple things.

Sandy from Chengdu, China says: I think people should quarantine at home and prepare to have enough food at home in order to make it through the quarantine. In China, the restaurants closed, and you couldn't even do delivery. People did hoard many of the supplies at the grocery store. They also hoarded masks. The scientists told us that wearing masks could help prevent the spread of the disease. 

Dennis from Shanghai, China says: I think people need to reduce unnecessary outside travel and avoid getting together. If you really need to go out, you must wear a mask to prevent the virus. The most important thing is to wash your hands regularly.
